Nim heaps in the Game of Cycles:
the parity conjecture fails on trees

Muchen Xu Address: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA Email address: xupeter@usc.edu
Date: October 2026
Abstract.

The Game of Cycles, invented by Francis Su, is a two-player game in which the players take turns drawing arrows on the edges of a plane graph, never creating a sink or a source. On a tree only the sink–source rule matters, and the player who makes the last move wins. Several authors conjectured that on a tree the second player wins exactly when the number of markable edges is even. We show that this parity conjecture is false, and we explain why.

The explanation is a hidden game of Nim: a path segment that is blocked by an arrow at one end and free at the other behaves exactly like a nim heap whose size is its length. Combined with a calculus for cutting and gluing trees at vertices next to leaves, this shows that the conjecture fails as soon as a single tree has Grundy value at least 22. The smallest counterexamples have 1515 vertices. Trees with Grundy values 22 and 44 first appear at 1717 vertices, and every value up to 6363 occurs, which answers a question of Fokkink and Zandee. We also refute a related conjecture of Zandee.

We then look closely at spiders. The spiders S⁡(2,3,z)S(2,3,z) violate the conjecture for every z≥14z\geq 14. The Grundy values of S⁡(1,2​j,z)S(1,2j,z) are given by an exact formula governed by binary carries. For 9999 pairs (x,y)(x,y), the value of S⁡(x,y,z)S(x,y,z) is eventually the parity of zz. On the positive side, the conjecture holds for all trees in which every thread has at most two edges, and this bound is sharp. Along the way we prove a twin-branch reduction, give an algorithm that is polynomial for spiders with a fixed number of legs, and collect the questions that we could not answer. The boldest asks whether every non-negative integer is the Grundy value of some tree.

Key words and phrases: 
Game of Cycles, Game of Arrows, impartial games, Sprague–Grundy theory, trees, spiders
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 91A46; Secondary 05C05, 05C57, 91A43

1. Introduction

The Game of Cycles was invented by Francis Su for his book Mathematics for Human Flourishing [15], and was first analysed by Alvarado et al. [3]. Two players take turns marking an unmarked edge of a plane graph with an arrow. One rule makes the game interesting: no vertex may ever become a sink, with all of its edges marked and pointing in, or a source, with all of its edges marked and pointing out. A player who completes a cycle cell, a bounded face whose boundary arrows all point the same way around it, wins at once. Otherwise the player who makes the last legal move wins.

It is a delightful game to show to someone. The rules fit on a napkin, a game on a small board takes a minute, and yet good play is far from obvious. It has been studied on cycles and symmetric graphs [3], three-legged spiders [11], grids and theta graphs [4] and cacti [1], as well as in variants [12]. Two theses examine it [10, 16], and a computer program decides small boards [7].

Anyone who plays a few games is tempted by a guess. On every board that Alvarado et al. solved, the first player wins exactly when the number of edges is odd. Lin [10, Conjecture 4.1] refined this to the number of markable edges. Boards with triangles turned out to break the rule [1, 6], but on trees the guess survived. A tree has no cells, so only the sink–source rule matters, and the game becomes a pure “last move wins” impartial game, which Mathews [11] called the Game of Arrows. An edge at a leaf can never be marked, since marking it would turn the leaf into a sink or a source. So the natural parameter of a tree TT is

m⁡(T)=#​{edges of T not incident to a leaf}.\operatorname{m}(T)=\#\{\text{edges of $T$ not incident to a leaf}\}.
Conjecture 1.1 (Parity Conjecture for trees; Lin [10], Zandee [16], Fokkink–Zandee [6]).

For every tree TT, the second player wins the Game of Arrows on TT if and only if m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) is even. Equivalently, the Grundy value of TT is 00 exactly when m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) is even.

The evidence was good. The conjecture is known in several cases:

  • •

    paths [10, 16, 12];

  • •

    trees that have no vertex of degree 22 once the pendant edges are removed [6, Theorem 1];

  • •

    trees in which every vertex of degree 22 is adjacent to a leaf [16, Theorem 4.2];

  • •

    three-legged spiders with two equal legs [10, Theorem 5.3];

  • •

    three-legged spiders all of whose legs have an even number of markable edges [11].

Fokkink and Zandee single out spiders as the difficult case. They also ask whether any graph has Grundy value 44 or more, the largest value they had found being 33 [6]. Lin asks for a “simple and nice winning strategy” on general three-legged spiders [10, Section 7.1].

A hidden game of Nim

The conjecture holds for all 54465446 trees with 22 to 1414 vertices. On 1515 vertices it fails, exactly twice, for the spiders S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) and S⁡(1,4,6)S(1,4,6) of Fig. 1. When the first counterexample appeared on the screen, our first reaction was suspicion, so we checked it with two independently written brute-force programs. Our second reaction was curiosity: why does parity fail here, after holding so stubbornly on thousands of smaller trees?

The answer is the heart of this paper, and it is pleasantly simple. Cut a leg of a spider somewhere in the middle. The part that falls off is a path whose inner end is now blocked by the new arrow and whose outer end is still free. Such a blocked path with kk edges behaves exactly like a nim heap of size kk (Theorem 4.3). So the Game of Arrows secretly contains Nim, with heaps of every size, and there is no reason for parity to decide anything. On S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) every first move leads to a position with Grundy value 22, 44, 66 or 88. In each case the second player has an answer, typically a cut that removes a heap of exactly the right size, and the first player loses (Table 3). On small trees the heaps are too short to matter, which is why the conjecture survives so long.

Once the nim heaps are visible, many things become possible. We can glue trees together and add their Grundy values, build trees with large Grundy values, prove that whole families of spiders violate the conjecture, and also prove that parity does win on trees without long paths of degree-22 vertices.

Main results

We use standard Sprague–Grundy theory, recalled in Section 2, and write g⁡(T)\operatorname{g}(T) for the Grundy value of the empty board on TT.

Main Theorem.
  1. (A)

    (Runs are nim heaps; Theorem 4.3.) Consider a path segment of kk unmarked edges whose interior vertices have degree 22. If one end of the segment is free and the other end is blocked by an arrow, the segment is equivalent to a nim heap of size kk. The three other boundary types have Grundy values in {0,1}\{0,1\}, given by explicit formulas.

  2. (B)

    (Splitting, gluing and reformulation; Section 5.) The game on TT is the disjunctive sum of the games on the pieces obtained by cutting TT at the vertices adjacent to leaves. Gluing two trees at such vertices nim-adds their Grundy values. Consequently, Conjecture 1.1 is equivalent to g⁡(T)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2 for every tree TT, and it fails as soon as a single tree has Grundy value at least 22.

  3. (C)

    (Twin branches; Theorem 5.6.) Suppose two branches at a vertex cc are isomorphic by a map fixing cc. Then replacing both by a single pendant edge at cc changes neither the Grundy value nor the parity of m\operatorname{m}. This recovers and extends the results for spiders with two equal legs.

  4. (D)

    (Counterexamples; Theorem 7.1.)

    • •

      The parity conjecture holds for every tree with at most 1414 vertices.

    • •

      On 1515 vertices there are exactly two counterexamples, the spiders S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) and S⁡(1,4,6)S(1,4,6), whose legs have 1,3,71,3,7 and 1,4,61,4,6 markable edges. Both have Grundy value 00 but 1111 markable edges.

    • •

      On 1717 vertices there are trees with Grundy values 22 and 44, and both are counterexamples.

  5. (E)

    (Large Grundy values; Theorem 7.3.) Every integer 0≤g≤630\leq g\leq 63 is the Grundy value of a tree; for example, the spider S⁡(17,90,95)S(17,90,95) has Grundy value 3232. This answers the question of Fokkink and Zandee in a strong form, already within the class of trees.

  6. (F)

    (Zandee’s second conjecture; Proposition 7.2.) Zandee conjectured that a tree with exactly one marked edge has Grundy value of the same parity as the number of remaining markable edges [16, Conjecture 4.3]. This fails already on 1212 vertices.

  7. (G)

    (Spider families; Theorems 8.1, 9.1 and 8.12.)

    • •

      g⁡(S⁡(2,3,z))=zmod2\operatorname{g}(S(2,3,z))=z\bmod 2 for all z≥14z\geq 14, so every such spider violates the parity conjecture.

    • •

      For j≥2j\geq 2 and z≥2​j+2z\geq 2j+2, g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,z))\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,z)) is given by an explicit formula involving binary carries. It is periodic in zz with least period 2⌈log2⁡j⌉+22^{\lceil\log_{2}j\rceil+2}, and it violates the conjecture for a positive proportion of zz.

    • •

      For 9999 pairs (x,y)(x,y), including (2,3)(2,3), g⁡(S⁡(x,y,z))=zmod2\operatorname{g}(S(x,y,z))=z\bmod 2 for all zz beyond an explicit threshold.

  8. (H)

    (Short threads; Corollaries 10.4 and 10.11.) If every thread of TT (a maximal path in a piece whose interior vertices have degree 22) has at most two edges, then g⁡(T)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2. This contains the theorems of Fokkink–Zandee and of Zandee on trees without long paths of degree-22 vertices. The bound is sharp: there is a counterexample on 2323 vertices whose threads have at most three edges.

A word on method

Much of this work was experimental in the best sense: compute, stare at the tables, guess, and then try to prove the guess. The proofs of (A)–(C), of the theorem on threads in (H), and of the formula for S⁡(1,2​j,z)S(1,2j,z) in (G) are by hand. The result on S⁡(2,3,z)S(2,3,z) is proved by hand apart from a finite check of 5252 explicit integer sequences. Parts (D)–(F), the rest of (G) and the sharpness example in (H) are computer-assisted, and we took care to make the computations trustworthy.

  • •

    All statements about trees with at most 2020 vertices were confirmed by a program that implements the raw rules of the game and uses none of our theory. For at most 1616 vertices, two such programs, written independently, were used. All of these statements were also confirmed by the theory-based solver of Proposition 3.7.

  • •

    The statements about larger spiders were confirmed by at least two independently written solvers based on Proposition 6.1.

  • •

    Statements about larger trees that are not spiders, such as the HH-shaped trees with large Grundy values in Section 11, rest on theory-based solvers, each confirmed by two independent implementations.

Table 1 lists which programs confirmed which claim, and all programs are available as ancillary files.

Organisation

Sections 2 and 3 set up the game and a convenient bookkeeping of positions. Section 4 contains the nim-heap computation, and Section 5 its structural consequences: gluing, the reformulation, and twin branches. Section 6 describes all positions of a spider and gives a polynomial-time algorithm, which partly addresses Lin’s question. Section 7 reports the experiments. Sections 8 and 9 prove the results on spider families, and Section 10 the theorem on short threads. We close in Section 11 with the questions we enjoyed most and could not answer. The boldest of them asks whether every non-negative integer is the Grundy value of some tree.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Impartial games

We use standard facts from combinatorial game theory; see [5, 2, 13]. A finite impartial game under the normal play convention (the player unable to move loses) has a Grundy value

g⁡(P)=mex⁡{g⁡(P′):P′​ an option of ​P},\operatorname{g}(P)=\operatorname{mex}\{\operatorname{g}(P^{\prime}):P^{\prime}\text{ an option of }P\},

where mex⁡S\operatorname{mex}S is the least non-negative integer not in SS. The second player wins from PP if and only if g⁡(P)=0\operatorname{g}(P)=0. In a disjunctive sum, a move is a move in exactly one component. The Sprague–Grundy theorem [14, 8] gives g⁡(P+Q)=g⁡(P)⊕g⁡(Q)\operatorname{g}(P+Q)=\operatorname{g}(P)\oplus\operatorname{g}(Q), where ⊕\oplus is bitwise exclusive or (nim-sum). A nim heap of size kk has Grundy value kk. Two games P,QP,Q satisfy g⁡(P)=g⁡(Q)\operatorname{g}(P)=\operatorname{g}(Q) if and only if P+QP+Q is a second-player win. This is the basis of the copycat argument in Theorem 5.6.

2.2. The Game of Arrows

Let TT be a finite tree. A position assigns to each edge either the label unmarked or one of its two orientations (an arc). A vertex vv is a sink (resp. source) if vv has at least one edge, all edges at vv are marked, and all of them point to (resp. away from) vv. A move orients one unmarked edge, and it is legal if afterwards neither endpoint of that edge is a sink or a source. We start from the empty position, and the player who makes the last legal move wins. We write g⁡(T)\operatorname{g}(T) for the Grundy value of the empty position.

A leaf is a vertex of degree 11, and an edge at a leaf is pendant. A vertex is special if it is not a leaf but is adjacent to a leaf.11 1 This is the “special vertex” of Fokkink and Zandee [6], created by trimming pendant edges.

Lemma 2.1.
  1. (a)

    A pendant edge can never be marked.

  2. (b)

    A special vertex can never become a sink or a source.

Proof.

Marking a pendant edge makes its leaf a source or a sink. Hence the pendant edge at a special vertex stays unmarked forever, so that vertex always keeps an unmarked edge. ∎

So the markable edges are the non-pendant ones, and m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) counts them. Figure 2 illustrates the rules.

A spider is a tree with exactly one vertex of degree at least 33, its centre. For integers k≥3k\geq 3 and x1,…,xk≥1x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\geq 1, we write S⁡(x1,…,xk)S(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}) for the spider whose tt-th leg is a path of xt+1x_{t}+1 edges. The last edge of each leg is pendant, so the leg has exactly xtx_{t} markable edges and m⁡(S⁡(x1,…,xk))=∑txt\operatorname{m}(S(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}))=\sum_{t}x_{t}. The spider has 1+∑t(xt+1)1+\sum_{t}(x_{t}+1) vertices. For example, S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) has legs of 2,4,82,4,8 edges and 1515 vertices (Fig. 1). A leg consisting of a single pendant edge would make the centre special, and then the spider splits into paths (see Corollary 5.5); this is why we assume xt≥1x_{t}\geq 1.

3. Positions as labelled forests

Whether a move is legal depends only on what is happening at its two endpoints. Before we can see any nim heaps, we need a good way to record this, and a way to break a position into independent pieces.

Definition 3.1.

Let PP be a position on TT and vv a vertex. Let d⁡(v)d(v) be the number of unmarked non-pendant edges at vv. The status s⁡(v)∈{𝗇,𝗂,𝗈,𝖿}s(v)\in\{\mathsf{n},\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o},\mathsf{f}\} is defined as follows.

  • •

    s⁡(v)=𝖿s(v)=\mathsf{f} (free) if vv is special, or if vv has both an incoming and an outgoing arc.

  • •

    Otherwise, s⁡(v)=𝗂s(v)=\mathsf{i} if vv has at least one incoming arc, s⁡(v)=𝗈s(v)=\mathsf{o} if vv has at least one outgoing arc, and s⁡(v)=𝗇s(v)=\mathsf{n} if vv has no arcs.

Lemma 3.2 (Legality).

Let u​vuv be an unmarked non-pendant edge. Orienting it as u→vu\to v is legal if and only if

(d⁡(u)≥2​ or ​s​(u)∈{𝗂,𝖿})and(d⁡(v)≥2​ or ​s​(v)∈{𝗈,𝖿}).\bigl(d(u)\geq 2\text{ or }s(u)\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{f}\}\bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl(d(v)\geq 2\text{ or }s(v)\in\{\mathsf{o},\mathsf{f}\}\bigr).

After the move, d⁡(u)d(u) and d⁡(v)d(v) decrease by one. The statuses update by s⁡(u)←s⁡(u)⋅𝗈s(u)\leftarrow s(u)\cdot\mathsf{o} and s⁡(v)←s⁡(v)⋅𝗂s(v)\leftarrow s(v)\cdot\mathsf{i}, where

𝗇⋅𝗈=𝗈,𝗂⋅𝗈=𝖿,𝗈⋅𝗈=𝗈,𝖿⋅𝗈=𝖿,𝗇⋅𝗂=𝗂,𝗂⋅𝗂=𝗂,𝗈⋅𝗂=𝖿,𝖿⋅𝗂=𝖿.\mathsf{n}\cdot\mathsf{o}=\mathsf{o},\quad\mathsf{i}\cdot\mathsf{o}=\mathsf{f},\quad\mathsf{o}\cdot\mathsf{o}=\mathsf{o},\quad\mathsf{f}\cdot\mathsf{o}=\mathsf{f},\qquad\mathsf{n}\cdot\mathsf{i}=\mathsf{i},\quad\mathsf{i}\cdot\mathsf{i}=\mathsf{i},\quad\mathsf{o}\cdot\mathsf{i}=\mathsf{f},\quad\mathsf{f}\cdot\mathsf{i}=\mathsf{f}.
Proof.

Only uu and vv change. After the move, uu has an outgoing arc, so it cannot be a sink; it is a source exactly when all of its edges are marked and none points into uu. If uu is special this never happens (Lemma 2.1), and s⁡(u)=𝖿s(u)=\mathsf{f}. Otherwise every edge at uu is non-pendant. Then all edges at uu are marked after the move if and only if d⁡(u)=1d(u)=1. Moreover, none points into uu if and only if uu had no incoming arc, i.e. s⁡(u)∈{𝗇,𝗈}s(u)\in\{\mathsf{n},\mathsf{o}\}. The argument for vv is symmetric. ∎

Thus the game from PP depends only on the reduced position: the forest F⁡(P)F(P) of unmarked non-pendant edges, in which every vertex carries its status. We formalise this as a game in its own right.

Definition 3.3.

A status-labelled forest is a finite forest FF together with a map s:V⁡(F)→{𝗇,𝗂,𝗈,𝖿}s\colon V(F)\to\{\mathsf{n},\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o},\mathsf{f}\}. The arrow game on (F,s)(F,s) has as moves the orientations u→vu\to v of edges u​vuv of FF that satisfy the condition of Lemma 3.2, where dd is the degree in FF. Such a move deletes the edge u​vuv and updates s⁡(u)s(u) and s⁡(v)s(v) as in Lemma 3.2.

By Lemma 3.2, the game from a position PP on TT is isomorphic to the arrow game on (F⁡(P),s)(F(P),s).

Lemma 3.4 (Dead edges).

Suppose an edge e=u​ve=uv of a status-labelled forest has no legal orientation. Then it has none after any sequence of moves. Consequently, deleting ee and setting s⁡(u)=s⁡(v)=𝖿s(u)=s(v)=\mathsf{f} does not change the game.

Proof.

Each orientation of ee is illegal because some endpoint ww has d⁡(w)=1d(w)=1 and an unsuitable status. For such ww, the edge ee is its only edge, so no move other than one on ee touches ww. Hence d⁡(w)d(w) and s⁡(w)s(w) are frozen, and ee stays illegal forever. Therefore ee is never deleted, so the condition at uu (and at vv) in Lemma 3.2 is satisfied for every other edge at uu (and at vv), because d≥2d\geq 2 there whenever another edge exists. This is exactly the effect of deleting ee and giving u,vu,v the status 𝖿\mathsf{f}, which also never changes. ∎

Lemma 3.5 (Splitting).

If s⁡(v)=𝖿s(v)=\mathsf{f}, the game is unchanged when vv is replaced by deg⁡(v)\deg(v) new vertices of status 𝖿\mathsf{f}, each incident with exactly one of the edges formerly at vv.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.2, the conditions at a vertex of status 𝖿\mathsf{f} always hold, and the status 𝖿\mathsf{f} never changes. ∎

Definition 3.6.

The normal form of a status-labelled forest is obtained by deleting dead edges (setting their endpoints to 𝖿\mathsf{f}), splitting every vertex of status 𝖿\mathsf{f}, and discarding isolated vertices. Its connected components, each regarded as an arrow game, are the components. The components of a position PP are those of (F⁡(P),s)(F(P),s).

Proposition 3.7.

Every position is the disjunctive sum of its components, so g⁡(P)=⨁Kg⁡(K)\operatorname{g}(P)=\bigoplus_{K}\operatorname{g}(K).

Proof.

By Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5, the normal form defines the same game as (F⁡(P),s)(F(P),s). Components share no vertices, and a move changes only the statuses of the endpoints of the deleted edge, which lie in one component. So legality in one component never depends on another. ∎

In the empty position, the status of a vertex is 𝖿\mathsf{f} if it is special and 𝗇\mathsf{n} otherwise, and there are no dead edges.22 2 An edge u​vuv with d⁡(u)=1d(u)=1 and s⁡(u)=𝗇s(u)=\mathsf{n} would force uu to have no other edges at all, since otherwise uu would be special. Then uu would be a leaf and u​vuv pendant. We call the components of the empty position the pieces of TT. They are obtained by deleting all pendant edges and cutting the tree at every special vertex. Every leaf of a piece has status 𝖿\mathsf{f}, and every other vertex has status 𝗇\mathsf{n} and the same degree as in TT.

Corollary 3.8.

g⁡(T)=⨁Qg⁡(Q)\operatorname{g}(T)=\bigoplus_{Q}\operatorname{g}(Q) and m⁡(T)=∑Q|E⁡(Q)|\operatorname{m}(T)=\sum_{Q}|E(Q)|, where QQ runs over the pieces of TT.

4. Runs: nim heaps inside the Game of Arrows

The basic components are paths, and the computation in this section is the key to almost everything that follows.

Definition 4.1.

Let k≥0k\geq 0 and α,β∈{∗,→,←}\alpha,\beta\in\{\ast,\rightarrow,\leftarrow\}. The run Rk​(α,β)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\alpha,\beta) is the arrow game on the status-labelled path v0v1⋯vkv_{0}v_{1}\cdots v_{k}, with edges ej=vj−1​vje_{j}=v_{j-1}v_{j}, in which the interior vertices have status 𝗇\mathsf{n}. The ends are determined by α\alpha and β\beta:

  • •

    α=∗\alpha=\ast means s⁡(v0)=𝖿s(v_{0})=\mathsf{f};

  • •

    α=→\alpha={\rightarrow} means s⁡(v0)=𝗂s(v_{0})=\mathsf{i}, so e1e_{1} may only be oriented v0→v1v_{0}\to v_{1};

  • •

    α=←\alpha={\leftarrow} means s⁡(v0)=𝗈s(v_{0})=\mathsf{o};

  • •

    symmetrically, β=∗,→,←\beta=\ast,\rightarrow,\leftarrow means s⁡(vk)=𝖿,𝗈,𝗂s(v_{k})=\mathsf{f},\mathsf{o},\mathsf{i}.

In words, ∗\ast is a free end, and an arrow is an end blocked in the indicated direction. The run R0\mathrm{R}_{0} is the empty game.

Lemma 4.2.

In Rk​(α,β)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\alpha,\beta), orienting eje_{j} in direction δ∈{→,←}\delta\in\{\rightarrow,\leftarrow\} is legal if and only if both of the following hold: j≠1j\neq 1 or α∈{∗,δ}\alpha\in\{\ast,\delta\}; and j≠kj\neq k or β∈{∗,δ}\beta\in\{\ast,\delta\}. The resulting game is Rj−1​(α,δ)+Rk−j​(δ,β)\mathrm{R}_{j-1}(\alpha,\delta)+\mathrm{R}_{k-j}(\delta,\beta).

Proof.

Interior vertices have d=2d=2, so by Lemma 3.2 only the ends impose conditions, and they are exactly the stated ones. Say δ=→\delta={\rightarrow}. Then vj−1v_{j-1} gains an outgoing arc. If j≥2j\geq 2, it becomes a vertex of status 𝗈\mathsf{o} with d=1d=1, which is a right end of type →\rightarrow for the path v0⋯vj−1v_{0}\cdots v_{j-1}. Likewise vjv_{j} becomes a left end of type →\rightarrow for vj⋯vkv_{j}\cdots v_{k}. If j=1j=1 (resp. j=kj=k), the end vertex becomes isolated and disappears. The case δ=←\delta={\leftarrow} is symmetric. ∎

Let α¯\bar{\alpha} denote α\alpha with the arrow reversed, where ∗¯=∗\bar{\ast}=\ast. Reflecting the path maps Rk​(α,β)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\alpha,\beta) to Rk​(β¯,α¯)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\bar{\beta},\bar{\alpha}), and reversing all arrows maps Rk​(α,β)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\alpha,\beta) to Rk​(α¯,β¯)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\bar{\alpha},\bar{\beta}). Both are isomorphisms of games. Composing them, Rk​(α,β)≅Rk​(β,α)≅Rk​(α¯,β¯)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\alpha,\beta)\cong\mathrm{R}_{k}(\beta,\alpha)\cong\mathrm{R}_{k}(\bar{\alpha},\bar{\beta}). Hence there are only four Grundy sequences:

Ak=gRk(∗,∗),Bk=gRk(∗,→),Ck=gRk(→,→),Dk=gRk(→,←).A_{k}=\operatorname{g}\mathrm{R}_{k}(\ast,\ast),\quad B_{k}=\operatorname{g}\mathrm{R}_{k}(\ast,\rightarrow),\quad C_{k}=\operatorname{g}\mathrm{R}_{k}(\rightarrow,\rightarrow),\quad D_{k}=\operatorname{g}\mathrm{R}_{k}(\rightarrow,\leftarrow).
Theorem 4.3 (Runs).

For every k≥0k\geq 0,

Ak=Ck=kmod2,Bk=k,Dk={1,k≥2​ even,0,otherwise.A_{k}=C_{k}=k\bmod 2,\qquad B_{k}=k,\qquad D_{k}=\begin{cases}1,&k\geq 2\text{ even},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

In particular, a run with one free end and one blocked end is equivalent to a nim heap whose size is its length.

Proof.

We use strong induction on kk. For k=0k=0 all four values are 00. Let k≥1k\geq 1 and assume the formulas for all smaller indices. By the induction hypothesis, for 1≤h<k1\leq h<k,

(1) Ch=hmod2,Dh=1−(hmod2),so{Ch,Dh}={0,1}.C_{h}=h\bmod 2,\qquad D_{h}=1-(h\bmod 2),\qquad\text{so}\qquad\{C_{h},D_{h}\}=\{0,1\}.

For h=1h=1 this reads C1=1C_{1}=1 and D1=0D_{1}=0. We use repeatedly that a⊕b≡a+b(mod2)a\oplus b\equiv a+b\pmod{2}. All options below come from Lemma 4.2.

AkA_{k}. Every move gives Bj−1⊕Bk−j=(j−1)⊕(k−j)B_{j-1}\oplus B_{k-j}=(j-1)\oplus(k-j), which is congruent to k−1k-1 modulo 22. If kk is even, all options are odd, so Ak=0A_{k}=0. If kk is odd, then j=(k+1)/2j=(k+1)/2 gives the option 00, and no option equals 11, so Ak=1A_{k}=1.

BkB_{k}. For 1≤j≤k−11\leq j\leq k-1, the two directions give Bj−1⊕Ck−jB_{j-1}\oplus C_{k-j} and Bj−1⊕Dk−jB_{j-1}\oplus D_{k-j}. By (1) these are j−1j-1 and (j−1)⊕1(j-1)\oplus 1. For j=kj=k only the direction →\rightarrow is legal, giving Bk−1=k−1B_{k-1}=k-1. So the set of options is

{j−1,(j−1)⊕1:1≤j≤k−1}∪{k−1}={0,1,…,k−1}.\{\,j-1,\ (j-1)\oplus 1:1\leq j\leq k-1\,\}\cup\{k-1\}=\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}.

Here every value 0,…,k−20,\dots,k-2 occurs as j−1j-1, and (j−1)⊕1≤j≤k−1(j-1)\oplus 1\leq j\leq k-1. Hence Bk=kB_{k}=k.

CkC_{k}. The edges e1e_{1} and eke_{k} may only be oriented →\rightarrow; interior edges may be oriented either way. The direction →\rightarrow gives Cj−1⊕Ck−jC_{j-1}\oplus C_{k-j}, which is congruent to (j−1)+(k−j)(j-1)+(k-j) modulo 22 (for j∈{1,k}j\in\{1,k\} one term is C0=0C_{0}=0). The direction ←\leftarrow at 2≤j≤k−12\leq j\leq k-1 gives Dj−1⊕Dk−jD_{j-1}\oplus D_{k-j}, which by (1) is also congruent to (j−1)+(k−j)(j-1)+(k-j) modulo 22. So every option equals (k−1)mod2(k-1)\bmod 2, and at least one option exists. Hence Ck=mex⁡{(k−1)mod2}=kmod2C_{k}=\operatorname{mex}\{(k-1)\bmod 2\}=k\bmod 2.

DkD_{k}. If k=1k=1, the only edge would have to be oriented both ways, so there is no move and D1=0D_{1}=0. Let k≥2k\geq 2. Orienting e1e_{1} (necessarily →\rightarrow) or eke_{k} (necessarily ←\leftarrow) gives Dk−1D_{k-1}. For 2≤j≤k−12\leq j\leq k-1, the options are Cj−1⊕Dk−jC_{j-1}\oplus D_{k-j} and Dj−1⊕Ck−jD_{j-1}\oplus C_{k-j}, and by (1) both equal 1⊕((k−1)mod2)=kmod21\oplus((k-1)\bmod 2)=k\bmod 2. If k=2k=2, the only option is D1=0D_{1}=0, so D2=1D_{2}=1. If k≥3k\geq 3, then Dk−1=1−((k−1)mod2)=kmod2D_{k-1}=1-((k-1)\bmod 2)=k\bmod 2 as well, so all options equal kmod2k\bmod 2 and Dk=1−(kmod2)D_{k}=1-(k\bmod 2). ∎

Corollary 4.4 (Paths).

A path with n≥3n\geq 3 vertices has g=(n−3)mod2=mmod2\operatorname{g}=(n-3)\bmod 2=\operatorname{m}\bmod 2. If n≥4n\geq 4 and one markable edge has been marked, the remaining position has Grundy value of the same parity as m−1=n−4\operatorname{m}-1=n-4. If the marked edge is one of the two end markable edges, the value is exactly n−4n-4.

Proof.

The path has a single piece Rn−3​(∗,∗)\mathrm{R}_{n-3}(\ast,\ast). Marking its jj-th edge leaves Rj−1​(∗,δ)+Rn−3−j​(δ,∗)\mathrm{R}_{j-1}(\ast,\delta)+\mathrm{R}_{n-3-j}(\delta,\ast), whose value is (j−1)⊕(n−3−j)≡n−4(mod2)(j-1)\oplus(n-3-j)\equiv n-4\pmod{2}, and which equals n−4n-4 when j∈{1,n−3}j\in\{1,n-3\}. ∎

Corollary 4.4 recovers [10, Theorem 5.1] and [16, Theorem 2.7, Corollary 2.8]. Zandee’s Theorem 2.7 is precisely the statement Bk=kB_{k}=k for runs arising from a path. The point of Theorem 4.3 is that every position on a tree decomposes into runs as soon as its branch vertices are resolved, and runs of type BB are nim heaps of unbounded size.

5. Splitting, gluing and twins

The run formulas have pleasant structural consequences. Vertices next to leaves act as hinges, where trees can be taken apart and glued together, and two identical branches at a vertex cancel each other out.

5.1. Gluing

Let T1,T2T_{1},T_{2} be trees with special vertices w1∈T1w_{1}\in T_{1} and w2∈T2w_{2}\in T_{2}. Let T1∘T2T_{1}\circ T_{2} denote the tree obtained from the disjoint union by identifying w1w_{1} with w2w_{2}. (The choice of w1,w2w_{1},w_{2} is suppressed from the notation.)

Theorem 5.1 (Gluing).

g⁡(T1∘T2)=g⁡(T1)⊕g⁡(T2)\operatorname{g}(T_{1}\circ T_{2})=\operatorname{g}(T_{1})\oplus\operatorname{g}(T_{2}) and m⁡(T1∘T2)=m⁡(T1)+m⁡(T2)\operatorname{m}(T_{1}\circ T_{2})=\operatorname{m}(T_{1})+\operatorname{m}(T_{2}).

Proof.

The merged vertex ww has degree at least 44 and is adjacent to a leaf, so it is special. Every other vertex keeps its neighbourhood. Therefore the leaves, the pendant edges and the special vertices of T1∘T2T_{1}\circ T_{2} are exactly those of T1T_{1} and T2T_{2}, with w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} merged. Deleting the pendant edges and cutting at the special vertices yields the pieces of T1T_{1} together with the pieces of T2T_{2}. Now apply Corollary 3.8. ∎

Remark 5.2.

A cheaper way to add 11: attach a path w​a​bw\,a\,b with two edges at a special vertex ww. This makes aa special, so the new markable edge w​awa forms a piece R1​(∗,∗)\mathrm{R}_{1}(\ast,\ast) by itself. The operation increases m\operatorname{m} by 11 and nim-adds 11 to the Grundy value, using only two new vertices.

Every tree with at least three vertices has a special vertex, and the trees with at most two vertices have Grundy value 00. Hence:

Corollary 5.3.

The set 𝒢={g⁡(T):T​ a finite tree}\mathcal{G}=\{\operatorname{g}(T):T\text{ a finite tree}\} is closed under ⊕\oplus, i.e. it is an 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-subspace of (ℕ,⊕)(\mathbb{N},\oplus). In particular, if 20,21,…,2r−1∈𝒢2^{0},2^{1},\dots,2^{r-1}\in\mathcal{G}, then {0,1,…,2r−1}⊆𝒢\{0,1,\dots,2^{r}-1\}\subseteq\mathcal{G}.

Proposition 5.4 (Reformulation).

The following are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    The parity conjecture holds for all trees.

  2. (ii)

    g⁡(T)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2 for every tree TT.

In particular, the parity conjecture implies g⁡(T)≤1\operatorname{g}(T)\leq 1 for all trees TT, so any single tree with Grundy value at least 22 refutes it.

Proof.

(ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i) is clear. Assume (i), and suppose some tree TT has g⁡(T)≠m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)\neq\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2. If m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) were even, (i) would give g⁡(T)=0\operatorname{g}(T)=0. So m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) is odd and g⁡(T)∉{0,1}\operatorname{g}(T)\notin\{0,1\}, i.e. g⁡(T)≥2\operatorname{g}(T)\geq 2. Let P4P_{4} be the path on four vertices, with m⁡(P4)=1\operatorname{m}(P_{4})=1 and g⁡(P4)=1\operatorname{g}(P_{4})=1. By Theorem 5.1, T∘P4T\circ P_{4} has an even number of markable edges and Grundy value g⁡(T)⊕1≠0\operatorname{g}(T)\oplus 1\neq 0, which contradicts (i). ∎

Note that a tree with g⁡(T)≥2\operatorname{g}(T)\geq 2 violates the conjecture itself if m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) is even. If m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) is odd, then T∘P4T\circ P_{4} violates it.

Corollary 5.5.

Suppose every vertex of degree at least 33 in TT is adjacent to a leaf; for instance, TT is a path, a caterpillar, or a spider whose centre is adjacent to a leaf. Then g⁡(T)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2.

Proof.

Every vertex of degree at least 33 is special, so all pieces are paths with free ends, i.e. runs Rk​(∗,∗)\mathrm{R}_{k}(\ast,\ast). By Corollaries 3.8 and 4.3, g⁡(T)=⨁Q(kQmod2)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\bigoplus_{Q}(k_{Q}\bmod 2)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2. ∎

5.2. Twin branches

Let cc be a vertex of TT. For a component BB of T−cT-c, let T⁡[B+c]T[B+c] denote the subtree induced by B∪{c}B\cup\{c\}. Two distinct components B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} of T−cT-c are twins at cc if there is a graph isomorphism φ:T⁡[B1+c]→T⁡[B2+c]\varphi\colon T[B_{1}+c]\to T[B_{2}+c] with φ⁡(c)=c\varphi(c)=c.

Theorem 5.6 (Twin branches).

Let B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} be twins at cc. Let T′T^{\prime} be obtained from TT by deleting B1∪B2B_{1}\cup B_{2} and attaching a new pendant edge at cc. Then g⁡(T)=g⁡(T′)\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{g}(T^{\prime}) and m⁡(T)≡m⁡(T′)(mod2)\operatorname{m}(T)\equiv\operatorname{m}(T^{\prime})\pmod{2}.

Proof.

We show that T+T′T+T^{\prime} is a second-player win. Let RR be the vertex set of TT outside B1∪B2B_{1}\cup B_{2}. The tree T⁡[R]T[R] appears both in TT and in T′T^{\prime}; let ψ\psi map each edge of T⁡[R]⊆TT[R]\subseteq T to the corresponding edge of T′T^{\prime}. Extend φ\varphi to an involution of B1∪B2∪{c}B_{1}\cup B_{2}\cup\{c\} by using φ−1\varphi^{-1} on B2B_{2}. After each of her moves, the second player maintains the following invariant.

  1. (1)

    For each edge ee of T⁡[B1+c]T[B_{1}+c], the edges ee and φ⁡(e)\varphi(e) are both unmarked, or both marked with opposite orientations: x→yx\to y on ee if and only if φ⁡(y)→φ⁡(x)\varphi(y)\to\varphi(x) on φ⁡(e)\varphi(e).

  2. (2)

    Every edge ee of T⁡[R]⊆TT[R]\subseteq T is in the same state as ψ⁡(e)\psi(e) in T′T^{\prime}.

The invariant holds at the start. When the first player marks an edge ee, the second player answers as follows.

  • •

    If ee lies in T⁡[B1+c]T[B_{1}+c] or T⁡[B2+c]T[B_{2}+c], she marks φ⁡(e)\varphi(e) with the opposite orientation.

  • •

    If ee lies in T⁡[R]⊆TT[R]\subseteq T, she marks ψ⁡(e)\psi(e) with the same orientation.

  • •

    If ee lies in T′T^{\prime}, she marks ψ−1​(e)\psi^{-1}(e) with the same orientation. (The new pendant edge of T′T^{\prime} is never marked.)

By the invariant the answering edge e∗e^{*} is unmarked, and afterwards the invariant holds again. It remains to show that the answer is legal, i.e. that neither endpoint of e∗e^{*} is a sink or a source afterwards.

Let w∗w^{*} be an endpoint of e∗e^{*} with w∗≠cw^{*}\neq c, and let ww be the corresponding endpoint of ee. The answering map (φ\varphi or ψ±1\psi^{\pm 1}) restricts to a bijection from the edges at ww to the edges at w∗w^{*}. The edge e∗e^{*} is not incident with ww, so after both moves the edges at w∗w^{*} are in the states, or in the reversed states in the twin case, of the edges at ww just after the first player’s legal move. So w∗w^{*} is neither a sink nor a source.

Now suppose cc is an endpoint of e∗e^{*}.

  • •

    If e∗e^{*} lies in T′T^{\prime}, then e∗∈ψ⁡(T⁡[R])e^{*}\in\psi(T[R]), so R≠{c}R\neq\{c\}. Hence cc has degree at least 22 in T′T^{\prime} and is adjacent to the new leaf, i.e. it is special. By Lemma 2.1 it is never a sink or source.

  • •

    If e∗e^{*} lies in TT, let bib_{i} be the neighbour of cc in BiB_{i}, so φ⁡(c​b1)=c​b2\varphi(cb_{1})=cb_{2}. After the answer, by the invariant, the edges c​b1cb_{1} and c​b2cb_{2} are either both unmarked, in which case cc keeps an unmarked edge, or marked with opposite orientations relative to cc, in which case cc has an incoming and an outgoing arc.

In every case the answer is legal. So the second player always has a reply, and since the game is finite she wins. Hence g⁡(T)⊕g⁡(T′)=0\operatorname{g}(T)\oplus\operatorname{g}(T^{\prime})=0.

For the parity statement, note that cc is not a leaf of TT, and the vertices of BiB_{i} have the same degree in TT as in T⁡[Bi+c]T[B_{i}+c]. So φ\varphi maps the edges of T⁡[B1+c]T[B_{1}+c] that are markable in TT bijectively onto those of T⁡[B2+c]T[B_{2}+c]. The new pendant edge of T′T^{\prime} is not markable. An edge of T⁡[R]T[R] at cc is markable in TT if and only if its image is markable in T′T^{\prime}; if R={c}R=\{c\} there are no such edges. Thus

m⁡(T)=m⁡(T′)+2​#​{edges of ​T​[B1+c]​ markable in ​T}.∎\operatorname{m}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T^{\prime})+2\,\#\{\text{edges of }T[B_{1}+c]\text{ markable in }T\}.\qed
Corollary 5.7.

For all x,z≥1x,z\geq 1, g⁡(S⁡(x,x,z))=zmod2\operatorname{g}(S(x,x,z))=z\bmod 2. More generally,

g⁡(S⁡(x,x,y1,…,yr))=(y1+⋯+yr)mod2.\operatorname{g}(S(x,x,y_{1},\dots,y_{r}))=(y_{1}+\dots+y_{r})\bmod 2.
Proof.

Replace the twin legs by a pendant edge. The centre becomes special, and the rest splits into the runs Ryt​(∗,∗)\mathrm{R}_{y_{t}}(\ast,\ast). ∎

The first statement is a Grundy-value form of Lin’s theorem on the spiders Ta,a,bT_{a,a,b} [10, Theorem 5.3]. Theorem 5.6 is also a tree analogue of the involution strategy of Alvarado et al. [3]. It shows that, as far as the parity conjecture is concerned, we may restrict attention to trees without twin branches.

6. Spiders

Spiders are where the action is. By Corollaries 5.5 and 5.6, the simplest pieces not covered so far are spiders with pairwise distinct legs and no leaf at the centre. We now describe all their positions. Fix the spider S⁡(x1,…,xk)S(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}) with centre cc.

6.1. Spider states

Directions on a leg are measured relative to the centre: in means towards cc, and out means away from cc. For s∈{𝗇,𝗂,𝗈,𝖿}s\in\{\mathsf{n},\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o},\mathsf{f}\} we write s⋅in=s⋅𝗂s\cdot\textup{{in}}=s\cdot\mathsf{i} and s⋅out=s⋅𝗈s\cdot\textup{{out}}=s\cdot\mathsf{o}; this is the status of cc after an arc at cc pointing into, respectively out of, cc (Lemma 3.2).

In any position, look along leg tt from the centre. Let hth_{t} be the number of unmarked edges before the first marked edge of the leg; if no edge of the leg is marked, count the unmarked edges before the pendant edge. The leg is attached if ht≥1h_{t}\geq 1, i.e. if its edge at cc is unmarked. The far end ϕt\phi_{t} of the attached part is ∗\ast if the leg contains no arc. Otherwise it is the direction (in or out) of the first arc, which by Lemma 4.2 forces the direction of the adjacent unmarked edge. Everything beyond the first arc on the leg splits into runs, whose values are given by Theorem 4.3.

A spider state is a pair (s;L)(s;L), where s∈{𝗇,𝗂,𝗈,𝖿}s\in\{\mathsf{n},\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o},\mathsf{f}\} is the status of cc and LL is the multiset of pairs (ht,ϕt)(h_{t},\phi_{t}) over the attached legs. While s=𝗇s=\mathsf{n}, all kk legs are attached.

For h≥0h\geq 0, δ∈{in,out}\delta\in\{\textup{{in}},\textup{{out}}\} and ϕ∈{∗,in,out}\phi\in\{\ast,\textup{{in}},\textup{{out}}\}, let ρ⁡(h,δ,ϕ)\rho(h;\delta,\phi) be the value of a detached run of hh edges whose near end is blocked in direction δ\delta and whose far end is ϕ\phi. By Theorem 4.3,

ρ(h;δ,∗)=Bh=h,ρ(h;δ,ϕ)=Ch if ϕ=δ,ρ(h;δ,ϕ)=Dh otherwise.\rho(h;\delta,\ast)=B_{h}=h,\qquad\rho(h;\delta,\phi)=C_{h}\text{ if }\phi=\delta,\qquad\rho(h;\delta,\phi)=D_{h}\text{ otherwise}.

Similarly, let ρ∗​(h,ϕ)\rho_{\ast}(h;\phi) be the value of a run with free near end and far end ϕ\phi. Thus ρ∗​(h,∗)=Ah\rho_{\ast}(h;\ast)=A_{h} and ρ∗​(h,in)=ρ∗​(h,out)=Bh\rho_{\ast}(h;\textup{{in}})=\rho_{\ast}(h;\textup{{out}})=B_{h}.

Let Γ⁡(s,L)\Gamma(s;L) be the Grundy value of the component containing cc. In the following degenerate cases it is given directly.

  1. (N1)

    If s=𝖿s=\mathsf{f}, then cc splits and every attached leg becomes a run with free near end, so Γ⁡(𝖿,L)=⨁(h,ϕ)∈Lρ∗​(h,ϕ)\Gamma(\mathsf{f};L)=\bigoplus_{(h,\phi)\in L}\rho_{\ast}(h;\phi).

  2. (N2)

    If s∈{𝗂,𝗈}s\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o}\} and L={(h,ϕ)}L=\{(h,\phi)\} has one element, the remaining edge at cc is forced (out if s=𝗂s=\mathsf{i}, in if s=𝗈s=\mathsf{o}). So Γ⁡(𝗂,L)=ρ⁡(h,out,ϕ)\Gamma(\mathsf{i};L)=\rho(h;\textup{{out}},\phi) and Γ⁡(𝗈,L)=ρ⁡(h,in,ϕ)\Gamma(\mathsf{o};L)=\rho(h;\textup{{in}},\phi).

  3. (N3)

    If L=∅L=\emptyset, then Γ=0\Gamma=0.

Proposition 6.1.

In the remaining cases (s=𝗇s=\mathsf{n}, or s∈{𝗂,𝗈}s\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o}\} with |L|≥2|L|\geq 2), Γ⁡(s,L)\Gamma(s;L) is the mex of the following option values. There is one option for each attached leg (h,ϕ)∈L(h,\phi)\in L, each 1≤j≤h1\leq j\leq h and each δ∈{in,out}\delta\in\{\textup{{in}},\textup{{out}}\}, except that δ=ϕ\delta=\phi is required when j=hj=h and ϕ≠∗\phi\neq\ast. Its value is

ρ⁡(h−j,δ,ϕ)⊕{Γ⁡(s,L−{(h,ϕ)}+{(j−1,δ)}),j≥2,Γ⁡(s⋅δ,L−{(h,ϕ)}),j=1.\rho(h-j;\delta,\phi)\ \oplus\ \begin{cases}\Gamma\bigl(s;\ L-\{(h,\phi)\}+\{(j-1,\delta)\}\bigr),&j\geq 2,\\[2.0pt] \Gamma\bigl(s\cdot\delta;\ L-\{(h,\phi)\}\bigr),&j=1.\end{cases}

The Grundy value of the spider is g⁡(S⁡(x1,…,xk))=Γ⁡(𝗇,{(x1,∗),…,(xk,∗)})\operatorname{g}(S(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}))=\Gamma(\mathsf{n};\{(x_{1},\ast),\dots,(x_{k},\ast)\}).

Proof.

Consider the move on the jj-th edge (from the centre) of the attached part of a leg, in direction δ\delta. It detaches the h−jh-j unmarked edges beyond it, which form a run blocked in direction δ\delta at the near end and with far end ϕ\phi. If j≥2j\geq 2, the part between cc and the new arc stays attached, with hh replaced by j−1j-1 and far end δ\delta. If j=1j=1, the arc is at cc and changes its status to s⋅δs\cdot\delta. The legality conditions come from Lemma 3.2. At cc there is no condition, because in the remaining cases cc has d⁡(c)=|L|≥2d(c)=|L|\geq 2. At the far end, the condition is δ=ϕ\delta=\phi when j=hj=h and ϕ≠∗\phi\neq\ast. Finally, apply Proposition 3.7. ∎

Corollary 6.2.

For each fixed kk, the Grundy value of a kk-legged spider with nn vertices can be computed in time O⁡(nk+1)O(n^{k+1}) and space O⁡(nk)O(n^{k}).

Proof.

There are at most 4​∏t(3​xt+1)=O⁡(nk)4\prod_{t}(3x_{t}+1)=O(n^{k}) spider states, each with O⁡(n)O(n) options. Each option is evaluated in constant time from Theorem 4.3 and memoised values. ∎

Remark 6.3 (How large values arise).

Cutting an attached leg with free far end at its jj-th edge creates the nim heap Rh−j(→,∗)\mathrm{R}_{h-j}(\rightarrow,\ast) of value h−jh-j. Hence, for 0≤t≤h−20\leq t\leq h-2, the options of the state include the numbers t⊕Γ⁡(s,L−{(h,∗)}+{(h−t−1,δ)})t\oplus\Gamma(s;\,L-\{(h,\ast)\}+\{(h-t-1,\delta)\}). If a long leg is cut near its middle, two large numbers of similar size are nim-added, and the result can be small. This is the mechanism behind the counterexamples, where a well-chosen cut produces an option of value 00 or of some other prescribed small value. The second player’s winning replies in Table 3 below are typically cuts of this kind.

7. Computations

Now for the experiments. The theory of the previous sections makes the search for counterexamples fast, and the computations in turn suggested most of the theorems proved in Sections 8, 9 and 10.

7.1. Programs and verification

All computations were made with the following programs. They are available as ancillary files (see the section on data and code availability at the end).

  1. (P1)

    Raw-rules solvers. These are two independently written programs, one in Python and one in C++. Positions are vectors in {unmarked,→,←}E⁡(T)\{\text{unmarked},\to,\leftarrow\}^{E(T)}, legality is checked literally (no vertex all-in or all-out), and Grundy values are memoised. No result of this paper is used.

  2. (P2)

    Normal-form solver for arbitrary trees. It implements Proposition 3.7, using canonical forms of status-labelled trees up to isomorphism and up to the global reversal 𝗂↔𝗈\mathsf{i}\leftrightarrow\mathsf{o}.

  3. (P3)

    Spider solvers implementing Proposition 6.1. There are four versions:

    • •

      an array-based C++ solver for three legs;

    • •

      a dictionary-based Python solver for three legs;

    • •

      a hash-based C++ solver for any number of legs;

    • •

      a solver for S⁡(x,y,z)S(x,y,z) with x,yx,y fixed and zz growing, which organises the recursion around the long leg.

    A fifth spider solver was written independently from the paper’s text alone.

In addition, the following cross-checks were made.

  • •

    The two raw-rules programs agree tree by tree on all 13,18713{,}187 trees with 22 to 1515 vertices.

  • •

    They agree with (P2) on all 22872287 trees with 22 to 1313 vertices.

  • •

    (P2) and (P3) agree on all three-legged spiders with legs at most 88 and all four-legged spiders with legs at most 44.

  • •

    The C++ and Python three-leg solvers agree on all 49604960 spiders with legs at most 3030.

  • •

    The array-based and fixed-x,yx,y solvers agree for all x≤6x\leq 6, y≤8y\leq 8, z≤120z\leq 120.

  • •

    The array-based and hash-based solvers agree on a random sample of 300300 spiders with legs at most 3030 and on the spiders used in Theorem 7.3.

For the counterexample S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7), the ancillary files also contain a certificate that can be checked by hand. It lists the values Γ\Gamma of all 205205 spider states reachable from the empty position, together with the values of their options. Verifying it requires only Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 6.1.

7.2. Census of small trees

For integers a1,a2,b1,b2≥1a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2}\geq 1 and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, let H⁡(a1,a2​|ℓ|​b1,b2)H(a_{1},a_{2}\,|\,\ell\,|\,b_{1},b_{2}) denote the tree with two branch vertices u,vu,v joined by a path of ℓ\ell edges. The vertex uu carries two further legs with a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} markable edges, and vv carries two legs with b1b_{1} and b2b_{2} markable edges; each leg ends with a pendant edge. All edges between uu and vv are markable, so m=a1+a2+b1+b2+ℓ\operatorname{m}=a_{1}+a_{2}+b_{1}+b_{2}+\ell, and the tree has a1+a2+b1+b2+ℓ+5a_{1}+a_{2}+b_{1}+b_{2}+\ell+5 vertices.

Theorem 7.1.
  1. (a)

    Every tree with at most 1414 vertices satisfies g⁡(T)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2.

  2. (b)

    Among the 77417741 trees with 1515 vertices, exactly two violate the parity conjecture: the spiders S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) and S⁡(1,4,6)S(1,4,6). Both have m=11\operatorname{m}=11 and g=0\operatorname{g}=0.

  3. (c)

    Every tree with at most 1616 vertices has Grundy value 00 or 11. Exactly two trees with 1717 vertices have larger Grundy value, namely the trees H⁡(3,1​| 3|​ 4,1)H(3,1\,|\,3\,|\,4,1) and H⁡(5,2​| 1|​ 3,1)H(5,2\,|\,1\,|\,3,1) of Fig. 3. Their Grundy values are 22 and 44, while m=12\operatorname{m}=12 for both, so both violate the parity conjecture.

  4. (d)

    The complete distribution of Grundy values for n≤20n\leq 20 is given in Table 2.

Table 3 lists every first move on S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) up to the global reversal of arrows. For each it gives the Grundy value of the resulting position and the winning replies of the second player. The legs are named X,Y,ZX,Y,Z, with 1,3,71,3,7 markable edges, as in Fig. 1. Edges are numbered from the centre, and in/out\textup{{in}}/\textup{{out}} are as in Section 6.

Every first move leads to a position with even, non-zero Grundy value. These values can be traced back to Theorem 4.3. For instance, after the first player plays Z4​outZ_{4}\textup{{out}}, the cut leaves the nim heap R3(→,∗)\mathrm{R}_{3}(\rightarrow,\ast) of value 33. The reply Z2​inZ_{2}\textup{{in}} then leaves a dead edge and a centre component of value 33, and the total nim-sum is 00.

7.3. Zandee’s conjecture on one marked edge

Zandee [16, Conjecture 4.3] conjectured the following. If a tree TT has exactly one marked edge, then the Grundy value of the resulting position has the same parity as m⁡(T)−1\operatorname{m}(T)-1. For paths this follows from Theorem 4.3 (see Corollary 4.4).

Proposition 7.2.

Zandee’s conjecture fails. In S⁡(1,3,4)S(1,3,4), which has 1212 vertices and m=8\operatorname{m}=8, mark the outermost markable edge of the leg with 33 markable edges, pointing away from the centre. The resulting position has Grundy value 44, but m−1=7\operatorname{m}-1=7 is odd. The trees S⁡(1,3,4)S(1,3,4) and S⁡(2,3,3)S(2,3,3) are the only counterexamples with at most 1212 vertices, and there are none with at most 1111 vertices.

In S⁡(2,3,3)S(2,3,3), marking the outermost markable edge of a leg with three markable edges gives the value 66. The parity conjecture itself holds for both trees: g⁡(S⁡(1,3,4))=g⁡(S⁡(2,3,3))=0\operatorname{g}(S(1,3,4))=\operatorname{g}(S(2,3,3))=0 and m=8\operatorname{m}=8. Note also that a counterexample to one of the two conjectures need not be a counterexample to the other. For instance, all first moves on the counterexample S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) lead to even values (Table 3), as Zandee’s conjecture predicts. By contrast, the other 1515-vertex counterexample S⁡(1,4,6)S(1,4,6) has a first move with the odd value 77, namely cutting its longest leg at the third edge, although m−1=10\operatorname{m}-1=10.

7.4. Large Grundy values

We computed g⁡(S⁡(x,y,z))\operatorname{g}(S(x,y,z)) for all 1≤x≤y≤z≤1201\leq x\leq y\leq z\leq 120, a total of 295,240295{,}240 spiders. The values 0,…,240,\dots,24, 26,27,28,30,3226,27,28,30,32 occur, and Table 4 lists the smallest example of each.

Theorem 7.3.

Every integer 0≤g≤630\leq g\leq 63 is the Grundy value of the Game of Arrows on some tree. In particular, there are trees with Grundy value 44 or larger, which answers the question of Fokkink and Zandee [6]. The smallest tree with Grundy value at least 22 has 1717 vertices, and the same holds for Grundy value 44.

Proof.

By Table 4, the values 1,2,4,8,16,321,2,4,8,16,32 are attained by the spiders S⁡(1,1,1)S(1,1,1), S⁡(3,4,7)S(3,4,7), S⁡(5,8,9)S(5,8,9), S⁡(7,12,19)S(7,12,19), S⁡(13,44,51)S(13,44,51) and S⁡(17,90,95)S(17,90,95). Write gg in binary and glue the corresponding spiders at special vertices. By Theorem 5.1 the resulting tree has Grundy value gg. The last statement is Theorem 7.1(c). ∎

Table 2 also shows that the value 33 first occurs only at 1818 vertices, later than the value 44; a smallest example is S⁡(2,3,9)S(2,3,9). The value 55 first occurs at 1919 vertices. An example is obtained from H⁡(5,2​| 1|​ 3,1)H(5,2\,|\,1\,|\,3,1) by attaching a path with two edges at a special vertex (Remark 5.2). Its pieces are the piece of H⁡(5,2​| 1|​ 3,1)H(5,2\,|\,1\,|\,3,1), of value 44, and a single edge, of value 11.

7.5. Families of spiders

For fixed x≤yx\leq y we computed z↦g⁡(S⁡(x,y,z))z\mapsto\operatorname{g}(S(x,y,z)) for 1≤z≤6001\leq z\leq 600. We did this for all 7878 pairs with 1≤x≤y≤121\leq x\leq y\leq 12 and for the 1414 pairs with x≤7x\leq 7 and y∈{13,14}y\in\{13,14\}, 9292 pairs in total. Table 5 summarises the results for y≤12y\leq 12. Three behaviours occur.

  1. (i)

    If x=yx=y, then Corollary 5.7 gives g=zmod2\operatorname{g}=z\bmod 2 for all zz.

  2. (ii)

    In all other computed pairs except those with x=1x=1 and yy even, there is a threshold z0​(x,y)z_{0}(x,y) such that

    g⁡(S⁡(x,y,z))=zmod2for all ​z0≤z≤600.\operatorname{g}(S(x,y,z))=z\bmod 2\qquad\text{for all }z_{0}\leq z\leq 600.

    Since m=x+y+z\operatorname{m}=x+y+z, the parity rule then holds for all such zz when x≡y(mod2)x\equiv y\pmod{2}, and fails for all such zz when x≢y(mod2)x\not\equiv y\pmod{2}. In the latter case the spider has Grundy value 11 with an even number of markable edges, or Grundy value 00 with an odd number. For example, S⁡(2,3,z)S(2,3,z) violates the parity conjecture for every 14≤z≤60014\leq z\leq 600. The thresholds are irregular; for instance z0​(1,3)=z0​(2,3)=14z_{0}(1,3)=z_{0}(2,3)=14, z0​(2,7)=34z_{0}(2,7)=34, z0​(1,9)=z0​(2,9)=56z_{0}(1,9)=z_{0}(2,9)=56, and the largest observed threshold is z0​(4,13)=70z_{0}(4,13)=70.

  3. (iii)

    If x=1x=1 and y=2y=2, then g=(z+1)mod2\operatorname{g}=(z+1)\bmod 2 for all computed zz, so the parity rule holds. If x=1x=1 and y≥4y\geq 4 is even, the sequence is periodic from early on, with period 88 for y=4y=4, 1616 for y∈{6,8}y\in\{6,8\}, and 3232 for y∈{10,12,14}y\in\{10,12,14\}. Within each period some values follow the parity rule and some violate it. For example, for z≥3z\geq 3 the values g⁡(S⁡(1,4,z))\operatorname{g}(S(1,4,z)) repeat the pattern 0,1,0,0,1,0,1,00,1,0,0,1,0,1,0, and the parity rule fails exactly when z≡0,1,2,6,7(mod8)z\equiv 0,1,2,6,7\pmod{8}.

These observations suggest the following conjecture.

Conjecture 7.4 (Eventual parity for spiders).

Let 1≤x≤y1\leq x\leq y with (x,y)(x,y) not of the form (1,2​j)(1,2j). Then g⁡(S⁡(x,y,z))=zmod2\operatorname{g}(S(x,y,z))=z\bmod 2 for all sufficiently large zz. Consequently, for all sufficiently large zz the spider S⁡(x,y,z)S(x,y,z) satisfies the parity conjecture if x≡y(mod2)x\equiv y\pmod{2} and violates it if x≢y(mod2)x\not\equiv y\pmod{2}.

In Section 8 we prove Conjecture 7.4 for (x,y)=(2,3)(x,y)=(2,3) by hand, apart from a finite computation, and, by a computer-assisted argument, for all 7373 computed pairs and for (2,y)(2,y) with y≤40y\leq 40. In Section 9 we determine g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,z))\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,z)) exactly, which explains behaviour (iii).

8. Eventual parity for spiders with two fixed legs

Tables are persuasive, but Table 5 stops at z=600z=600. In this section we cross that finite horizon and prove Conjecture 7.4 for the pair (x,y)=(2,3)(x,y)=(2,3). This gives an infinite, twin-free family of counterexamples to the parity conjecture. The proof is by hand, except that 5252 explicit integer sequences are checked by computer on a finite range, and one small constant is computed.

In Section 8.4 we isolate the finitely many facts the argument needs, so that a program can check them for other pairs. This proves Conjecture 7.4 for all 7373 pairs computed in Section 7.5 that are neither twins nor of the form (1,even)(1,\text{even}), and also for (2,y)(2,y) with y≤40y\leq 40 (Theorem 8.12). The thresholds observed in Table 5 for z≤600z\leq 600 therefore hold for all zz. The excluded family (1,2​j)(1,2j) is solved completely, by hand, in Section 9.

Theorem 8.1.

For every z≥14z\geq 14,

g⁡(S⁡(2,3,z))=zmod2.\operatorname{g}(S(2,3,z))=z\bmod 2.

Consequently, for every z≥14z\geq 14 the spider S⁡(2,3,z)S(2,3,z) violates the parity conjecture. It has m=z+5\operatorname{m}=z+5 markable edges, and its Grundy value is 00 when m\operatorname{m} is odd and 11 when m\operatorname{m} is even. The bound is sharp: g⁡(S⁡(2,3,13))=0\operatorname{g}(S(2,3,13))=0.

8.4. A finite certificate for other pairs

The proof of Theorem 8.1 has three ingredients. First, closed forms for all blocked families. Second, a propagation argument that extends them from a finite range to all rr. Third, lower bounds for a few free families, obtained from explicit cuts. We now state these ingredients for an arbitrary pair, in a form that a program can check.

9. The family S⁡(1,2​j,z)S(1,2j,z)

The family S⁡(1,2​j,z)S(1,2j,z) refused to follow Conjecture 7.4. It turns out to obey a different and prettier rule, governed by the carries in binary addition. We find an exact formula for g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,z))\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,z)), proved entirely by hand. It explains the periods 8,16,328,16,32 of Table 5, and it shows that each such family contains infinitely many counterexamples to the parity conjecture.

Throughout, ⊕\oplus is nim-addition, &\mathbin{\&} is bitwise AND, and [P]∈{0,1}[P]\in\{0,1\} is the truth value of a statement PP. For δ∈{in,out}\delta\in\{\textup{{in}},\textup{{out}}\} let δ¯\bar{\delta} be the other direction. For j≥1j\geq 1 put

Sj={b≥0:b&(j−1)=0}.S_{j}=\{\,b\geq 0:b\mathbin{\&}(j-1)=0\,\}.

Thus b∈Sjb\in S_{j} if and only if the binary addition b+(j−1)b+(j-1) has no carry, i.e. b+(j−1)=b⊕(j−1)b+(j-1)=b\oplus(j-1); equivalently, (b+j−1b)\binom{b+j-1}{b} is odd. Membership in SjS_{j} depends only on bmod2⌈log2⁡j⌉b\bmod 2^{\lceil\log_{2}j\rceil}.

Theorem 9.1.
  1. (a)

    g⁡(S⁡(1,2,z))=(z+1)mod2\operatorname{g}(S(1,2,z))=(z+1)\bmod 2 for all z≥1z\geq 1.

  2. (b)

    Let j≥2j\geq 2 and z≥2​j+2z\geq 2j+2. Write z−2​j+2=4​b+rz-2j+2=4b+r with 0≤r≤30\leq r\leq 3. Then

    g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,z))={[r=2]if ​b∈Sj,zmod2if ​b∉Sj.\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,z))=\begin{cases}[\,r=2\,]&\text{if }b\in S_{j},\\ z\bmod 2&\text{if }b\notin S_{j}.\end{cases}

    Equivalently: for even zz, g=1\operatorname{g}=1 if and only if z≡2​j(mod4)z\equiv 2j\pmod{4} and z−2​j4∈Sj\tfrac{z-2j}{4}\in S_{j}; for odd zz, g=1\operatorname{g}=1 if and only if ⌊z−2​j+24⌋∉Sj\lfloor\tfrac{z-2j+2}{4}\rfloor\notin S_{j}.

In words: cut the values z=2​j−2,2​j−1,…z=2j-2,2j-1,\dots into consecutive blocks of four, numbered b=0,1,2,…b=0,1,2,\dots. The bb-th block of Grundy values reads 0,0,1,00,0,1,0 if b∈Sjb\in S_{j}, and 0,1,0,10,1,0,1 otherwise. The theorem proves this for the blocks with b≥1b\geq 1. By Remark 9.8 it also holds for b=0b=0 in all computed cases with j≥3j\geq 3.

Corollary 9.2.

Let j≥2j\geq 2 and N=2⌈log2⁡j⌉N=2^{\lceil\log_{2}j\rceil} (the least power of 22 that is ≥j\geq j). On z≥2​j+2z\geq 2j+2 the sequence z↦g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,z))z\mapsto\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,z)) is periodic with least period 4​N=2⌈log2⁡j⌉+24N=2^{\lceil\log_{2}j\rceil+2}. The spider S⁡(1,2​j,z)S(1,2j,z), z≥2​j+2z\geq 2j+2, satisfies the parity conjecture if and only if z≡2​j−1, 2​j, 2​j+1(mod4)z\equiv 2j-1,\,2j,\,2j+1\pmod{4} and b∈Sjb\in S_{j} (with bb as in Theorem 9.1). The density of violations is 1−34⋅2−s⁡(j−1)1-\tfrac{3}{4}\cdot 2^{-s(j-1)}, where s⁡(n)s(n) is the binary digit sum of nn.

Proof.

Put χ(b)=[b∈Sj]\chi(b)=[b\in S_{j}]. Since N/2<j≤NN/2<j\leq N, we have N/2≤j−1<NN/2\leq j-1<N, so χ\chi depends only on bmodNb\bmod N, and χ⁡(0)=1\chi(0)=1, χ⁡(N/2)=0\chi(N/2)=0. Thus 4​N4N is a period. The least period of χ\chi is NN. Indeed, let qq be an eventual period of χ\chi and d=gcd⁡(q,N)d=\gcd(q,N). Then χ\chi is dd-periodic: write d=u​q−v​Nd=uq-vN with integers u,v≥0u,v\geq 0; for every bb and every large ww we get χ⁡(b+d)=χ⁡(b+d+w​N)=χ⁡(b+(w−v)​N)=χ⁡(b)\chi(b+d)=\chi(b+d+wN)=\chi(b+(w-v)N)=\chi(b). Here the middle step applies the eventual qq-periodicity uu times. So dd is a power of 22 dividing NN. If d≤N/2d\leq N/2 then χ⁡(N/2)=χ⁡(0)=1\chi(N/2)=\chi(0)=1, a contradiction. Hence N|qN\mid q.

Now let pp be a period of z↦g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,z))z\mapsto\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,z)) on z≥z0z\geq z_{0}. By Theorem 9.1, an odd zz has value 11 exactly when χ⁡(b)=0\chi(b)=0, and an even zz has value 11 exactly when r=2r=2 and χ⁡(b)=1\chi(b)=1.

Suppose pp is odd. Take a large block bb with χ⁡(b)=0\chi(b)=0. Its elements z1z_{1} (with r=1r=1) and z1+2z_{1}+2 (with r=3r=3) both have value 11. So the even numbers z1+pz_{1}+p and z1+2+pz_{1}+2+p have value 11, hence both have r=2r=2. This is absurd, since they differ by 22.

So pp is even. If p≡2(mod4)p\equiv 2\pmod{4}, comparing odd zz with r=1r=1 and with r=3r=3 gives χ⁡(b)=χ⁡(b+p−24)=χ⁡(b+p+24)\chi(b)=\chi(b+\frac{p-2}{4})=\chi(b+\frac{p+2}{4}) for all large bb. The two shifts differ by 11, so χ⁡(b′+1)=χ⁡(b′)\chi(b^{\prime}+1)=\chi(b^{\prime}) for all large b′b^{\prime}, i.e. χ\chi is eventually constant, which it is not. (This also covers p=2p=2.) Hence 4|p4\mid p, and odd zz give χ⁡(b)=χ⁡(b+p/4)\chi(b)=\chi(b+p/4) for all large bb. So N|p/4N\mid p/4.

For the parity statement note m⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,z))=2​j+1+z≡z+1\operatorname{m}(S(1,2j,z))=2j+1+z\equiv z+1, and g∈{0,1}\operatorname{g}\in\{0,1\}, so the conjecture holds if and only if g=(z+1)mod2\operatorname{g}=(z+1)\bmod 2. Since |Sj∩[0,N)|=N​ 2−s⁡(j−1)|S_{j}\cap[0,N)|=N\,2^{-s(j-1)}, the density of such zz is 34​2−s⁡(j−1)\tfrac{3}{4}2^{-s(j-1)}. ∎

Remark 9.8.

The proof needs z≥2​j+2z\geq 2j+2 mainly to exclude the options (a)–(d). By machine computation (two independent programs), the formula of Theorem 9.1(b) holds for all z≥2​j−2z\geq 2j-2 when 3≤j≤803\leq j\leq 80, and for all z≥3z\geq 3 when j=2j=2. For 3≤j≤803\leq j\leq 80 we also have g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,2​j−3))≠g⁡(S⁡(1,2​j,2​j−3+4​N))\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,2j-3))\neq\operatorname{g}(S(1,2j,2j-3+4N)) with NN as in Corollary 9.2, so the sequence is purely periodic from z=2​j−2z=2j-2 and not from z=2​j−3z=2j-3.

Remark 9.9 (Why x=1x=1 is special).

For every pair covered by Theorem 8.12, the computations behind it show that the blocked family Γ⁡(𝗇,(x,∗),(y,∗),(t,δ))\Gamma(\mathsf{n};(x,\ast),(y,\ast),(t,\delta)) is eventually t+ct+c with cc even. The long-leg cuts then all have the parity of z−1z-1, as in the proof of Theorem 8.1. For x=1x=1 and even yy, Lemma 9.7 shows instead that the shift Λ⁡(t)−t\Lambda(t)-t oscillates with tt in a 22-adic pattern. The correction εj\varepsilon_{j} comes from a single option: cutting the leg with yy markable edges at its first edge gives (y−1)⊕γδ​(t)(y-1)\oplus\gamma_{\delta}(t). Here γδ​(t)∈{t−1,t+1}\gamma_{\delta}(t)\in\{t-1,t+1\} grows linearly because marking the edge of the leg with one markable edge frees the centre and turns the blocked leg into a nim heap (Lemma 9.4).

10. Short threads

So far we have mostly broken things. In this section parity wins. A thread is a maximal path in a piece whose interior vertices have degree 22. Every run that occurs in a position lies inside a thread, so short threads leave no room for large nim heaps, and one may hope that parity survives. It does: the parity conjecture holds for all trees whose threads have at most two edges. The bound is sharp, since there are counterexamples all of whose threads have at most three edges, although every counterexample with at most 2222 vertices has a thread with at least 44 edges (Theorem 10.11).

10.1. Clean and almost clean trees

The proof is a strategy argument. We find a class 𝒞\mathcal{C} of status-labelled trees, containing all pieces of such trees, such that every move from a member of 𝒞\mathcal{C} leaves a sum of members of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, possibly after a single reply (Lemma 10.9). Induction on the number of edges then does the rest.

Throughout, XX denotes a status-labelled tree in normal form (Definition 3.6) in which no leaf has status 𝗇\mathsf{n}. This holds for every component of every position: a vertex of status 𝗇\mathsf{n} has not lost any edge, and the non-leaf vertices of a piece have degree at least 22. A leaf is free if its status is 𝖿\mathsf{f} and blocked otherwise. We write d⁡(x)d(x) for the degree of xx in XX. A chain edge is an edge both of whose ends have degree 22. For θ∈{𝗂,𝗈}\theta\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o}\} we say that a vertex receives type θ\theta when a move gives it an incoming (θ=𝗂\theta=\mathsf{i}) or outgoing (θ=𝗈\theta=\mathsf{o}) arc; its status then becomes s⋅θs\cdot\theta (Lemma 3.2). We write θ¯\bar{\theta} for the other type. For an edge c​rcr let Xr|cX_{r|c} be the component of X−c​rX-cr containing rr.

Definition 10.1.

XX is clean if all its leaves are free and it has no chain edge. XX is almost clean with defect ww if s⁡(w)∈{𝗂,𝗈}s(w)\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o}\} and

  1. (C1)

    every leaf other than ww is free;

  2. (C2)

    every chain edge is incident with ww;

  3. (C3)

    if ww is a leaf, then its neighbour has degree at least 33.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the class of trees XX that are clean, almost clean, or have at most one edge. A 𝒞\mathcal{C}-sum is a position whose components all lie in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

The pieces of a tree TT have free leaves and all other vertices of status 𝗇\mathsf{n}. Two adjacent vertices of degree 22 in a piece are interior vertices of a common thread. Hence:

Observation 10.2.

All threads of TT have at most two edges if and only if every piece of TT is clean.

Theorem 10.3.

Every X∈𝒞X\in\mathcal{C} satisfies g⁡(X)=|E⁡(X)|mod2\operatorname{g}(X)=|E(X)|\bmod 2. In particular, every clean status-labelled tree (with arbitrary statuses 𝗇,𝗂,𝗈\mathsf{n},\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o} on its non-leaf vertices) satisfies g⁡(X)=|E⁡(X)|mod2\operatorname{g}(X)=|E(X)|\bmod 2.

Corollary 10.4.

Let TT be a tree all of whose threads have at most two edges. Then g⁡(T)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2, so the parity conjecture holds for TT. Moreover, every position obtained from TT by a single move has Grundy value (m⁡(T)−1)mod2(\operatorname{m}(T)-1)\bmod 2. In particular Zandee’s conjecture [16, Conjecture 4.3] holds for TT, and if m⁡(T)\operatorname{m}(T) is odd then every first move on TT is a winning move.

Proof.

By Observation 10.2 all pieces are clean, so Corollary 3.8 and Theorem 10.3 give g⁡(T)=m⁡(T)mod2\operatorname{g}(T)=\operatorname{m}(T)\bmod 2. A first move lies in one piece QQ; by Lemma 10.9(ii) below (clean case) it turns QQ into a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-sum with |E⁡(Q)|−1|E(Q)|-1 edges, whose value is (|E⁡(Q)|−1)mod2(|E(Q)|-1)\bmod 2 by Theorem 10.3. The other pieces are unchanged. ∎

Corollary 10.4 contains the theorem of Fokkink and Zandee [6, Theorem 1] (no vertex of degree 22 once the pendant edges are removed) and Zandee’s theorem on trees in which every vertex of degree 22 is adjacent to a leaf [16, Theorem 4.2]: in both cases all threads have one edge.

10.2. Three lemmas

Lemma 10.5.

Let FF be a status-labelled forest with no vertex of status 𝗇\mathsf{n} and degree 11. An edge x​yxy of FF has no legal orientation if and only if d⁡(x)=d⁡(y)=1d(x)=d(y)=1 and s⁡(x)=s⁡(y)∈{𝗂,𝗈}s(x)=s(y)\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o}\}.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.2, an end of degree at least 22, or of status 𝖿\mathsf{f}, never forbids an orientation, and a blocked end of degree 11 forbids exactly one orientation: the one in which it would receive a second arc of its own type. So both orientations are forbidden exactly when both ends are blocked leaves forbidding opposite orientations, i.e. when they have the same status. ∎

In particular, no component with at least two edges, and no single edge with a free end, contains a dead edge. In all positions considered below, single-edge components have a free end, so normalising never deletes edges, and every move decreases the total number of edges by exactly one.

Lemma 10.6 (Opposite blocked neighbour).

Let zz be a blocked leaf with neighbour vv, where s⁡(v)∈{𝗂,𝗈}s(v)\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o}\} and s⁡(v)≠s⁡(z)s(v)\neq s(z). Changing s⁡(v)s(v) to 𝖿\mathsf{f} does not change the game.

Proof.

The only legal orientation of v​zvz gives vv an arc of type s⁡(v)¯\overline{s(v)}: if s⁡(z)=𝗂s(z)=\mathsf{i} then v​zvz must be oriented z→vz\to v and s⁡(v)=𝗈s(v)=\mathsf{o}, and symmetrically. Consider any sequence of moves. While v​zvz is unmarked, vv has at least two unmarked edges whenever another edge at vv is oriented, so the condition at vv in Lemma 3.2 holds. When v​zvz is oriented, vv receives the type it lacks, so the condition at vv holds and vv gets status 𝖿\mathsf{f}. Afterwards s⁡(v)=𝖿s(v)=\mathsf{f}. So the condition at vv always holds, exactly as if s⁡(v)=𝖿s(v)=\mathsf{f}, and the statuses of all other vertices do not depend on s⁡(v)s(v). ∎

Lemma 10.7 (One modified vertex).

Let a​bab be an edge of XX and A=Xa|bA=X_{a|b}. Suppose that every leaf of XX lying in A−aA-a is free and that no edge of AA is a chain edge of XX. Let θ∈{𝗂,𝗈}\theta\in\{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{o}\}, and let AθA^{\theta} be AA with s⁡(a)s(a) replaced by s⁡(a)⋅θs(a)\cdot\theta. Then the normal form of AθA^{\theta} is a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-sum with |E⁡(A)||E(A)| edges.

Proof.

All vertices of AA other than aa have the same degree in AA as in XX, and dA​(a)=d⁡(a)−1d_{A}(a)=d(a)-1. If s⁡(a)⋅θ=𝖿s(a)\cdot\theta=\mathsf{f}, splitting aa (Lemma 3.5) yields the components of A−aA-a, each with a free leaf attached in place of aa; their leaves are free and they have no chain edge, so they are clean or single edges. Otherwise s⁡(a)⋅θ=θs(a)\cdot\theta=\theta. If d⁡(a)=1d(a)=1 then AA has no edge. If d⁡(a)=2d(a)=2, then aa is a blocked leaf of AθA^{\theta}; its neighbour zz satisfies d⁡(z)≠2d(z)\neq 2 because a​zaz is not a chain edge of XX. If d⁡(z)=1d(z)=1 then zz is free and AθA^{\theta} is a single edge with a free end; if d⁡(z)≥3d(z)\geq 3 then AθA^{\theta} is almost clean with defect aa. If d⁡(a)=3d(a)=3, then aa has degree 22 and status θ\theta, all leaves are free, and every chain edge of AθA^{\theta} is incident with aa; so AθA^{\theta} is almost clean with defect aa. If d⁡(a)≥4d(a)\geq 4 then AθA^{\theta} is clean. By Lemma 10.5 there are no dead edges. ∎

Lemma 10.8.

Let XX be almost clean with defect ww.

  1. (a)

    If c​rcr is an edge with w∉Xr|cw\notin X_{r|c}, then the hypotheses of Lemma 10.7 hold for the edge r​crc and A=Xr|cA=X_{r|c}.

Then splitting cc turns YY (with a free leaf in place of cc) into an almost clean tree with defect ww or a single edge with a free end, and turns every other component of X−cX-c whose edges and statuses are unchanged into a clean tree or a single edge with a free end.

(a) Every leaf of XX in Xr|cX_{r|c} is free by (C1), and every chain edge of XX is incident with ww by (C2), so none lies in Xr|cX_{r|c}. Let X∈𝒞X\in\mathcal{C} have at least one edge, and put e=|E⁡(X)|e=|E(X)|.

Induction on e=|E⁡(X)|e=|E(X)|; the case e=0e=0 is trivial. By induction and the Sprague–Grundy theorem, a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-sum with k<ek<e edges has value kmod2k\bmod 2. The vertex zz has at least two neighbours other than aa, and at most one of them, q′q^{\prime}, has w∈Xq′|zw\in X_{q^{\prime}|z}. Choose a neighbour q∉{a,q′}q\notin\{a,q^{\prime}\}. The reply is to orient z​qzq so that zz receives type π¯\bar{\pi}. This is legal at zz, because a​zaz is still unmarked, and legal at qq. Now zz has status 𝖿\mathsf{f}, or status π¯\bar{\pi} next to the blocked leaf aa of status π\pi; in both cases zz is 𝖿\mathsf{f} by Lemma 10.6. What remains is the single edge a​zaz with a free end, Xq|zX_{q|z} with qq modified (Lemma 10.8(a) and Lemma 10.7), the component containing ww (Lemma 10.8(b)), and clean trees.

In every case, by Lemma 10.5 no edge is deleted by normalisation. So the position after the first move has e−1e-1 edges, and after a reply it has e−2e-2 edges. ∎

Remark 10.10.

The class 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the strategy were found with the help of a computer: we searched for a class of positions containing all clean trees that is closed under “a move, followed by a reply when needed”. The strategy in the proof was then implemented literally by an independent program. It was checked on all 740,508740{,}508 positions of 𝒞\mathcal{C} with at most 1212 vertices, counted up to isomorphism, and on all of their 15,385,70315{,}385{,}703 first moves, for every case and every admissible choice in the proof. The Grundy values of all these positions equal |E|mod2|E|\bmod 2. Moreover, every tree with at most 1818 vertices whose threads have at most two edges satisfies Corollary 10.4, including the statement about first moves.

10.4. Threads of length three

Theorem 10.11.

There are trees all of whose threads have at most three edges that violate the parity conjecture. The smallest have 2323 vertices. For example, let T21T_{21} be the following tree with 2121 vertices and m=15\operatorname{m}=15. Vertices uu and vv are joined by a path with 33 edges. The vertex uu carries two legs with 22 and 33 markable edges. The vertex vv carries a leg with 22 markable edges and is adjacent to a vertex ww, which carries two legs with 11 and 33 markable edges. Each leg ends with a pendant edge. Then g⁡(T21)=3\operatorname{g}(T_{21})=3, and attaching a path with two edges at a special vertex (Remark 5.2) gives a tree T23T_{23} with 2323 vertices, m=16\operatorname{m}=16 and g=2\operatorname{g}=2. There are also four trees with 2525 vertices, m=18\operatorname{m}=18 and g=2\operatorname{g}=2 consisting of a single piece with threads of at most three edges.

The values were computed by three programs: a raw-rules solver applied to the actual trees T21T_{21} and T23T_{23}, the normal-form solver (P2), and a third, independently written normal-form solver. The minimality was established in two independent ways.

  • •

    An exhaustive enumeration of all trees with at most 2323 vertices whose threads have at most three edges (4,075,7374{,}075{,}737 such trees with 2222 vertices, 14,828,07414{,}828{,}074 with 2323). It finds no counterexample with at most 2222 vertices, and exactly five with 2323 vertices, all with m=16\operatorname{m}=16 and g=2\operatorname{g}=2.

  • •

    A search over pieces. A counterexample must contain a piece QQ with g⁡(Q)≠|E⁡(Q)|mod2\operatorname{g}(Q)\neq|E(Q)|\bmod 2. The copycat argument of Theorem 5.6 also works for pieces, whose vertices have status 𝗇\mathsf{n} or 𝖿\mathsf{f}, so we may assume that QQ has no twin branches. Among the twin-free pieces with threads of at most three edges and at most 1818 vertices, the piece of T21T_{21} is the only such QQ.

11. Conjectures and open problems

Many questions remain open. Here are the ones we found hardest to put down.

Conjecture 11.1 (Unbounded Grundy values).

The Grundy values of the Game of Arrows on trees are unbounded. In fact 𝒢=ℕ\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{N}: every non-negative integer is the Grundy value of some tree.

Since 𝒢\mathcal{G} is an 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-subspace (Corollary 5.3), 𝒢=ℕ\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{N} holds if and only if for every r≥0r\geq 0 some tree has a Grundy value in [2r,2r+1)[2^{r},2^{r+1}), because elements with distinct leading bits span everything. We know this for r≤5r\leq 5 (Theorem 7.3).

As evidence, the maximum Grundy value over three-legged spiders with legs of at most LL markable edges grows steadily: it is 1313 for L=30L=30, 2828 for L=80L=80, 3232 for L=120L=120 and 4444 for L=300L=300, the last attained by S⁡(33,215,218)S(33,215,218). Trees with two branch vertices reach larger values with fewer edges. For instance, H⁡(8,13​| 23|​ 17,23)H(8,13\,|\,23\,|\,17,23) has value 3232 with m=84\operatorname{m}=84, and H⁡(6,41​| 19|​ 19,39)H(6,41\,|\,19\,|\,19,39) has value 6262 with m=124\operatorname{m}=124; both were confirmed by two independent programs. Large values seem to require long legs of similar lengths, in line with Remark 6.3.

A natural strategy for proving Conjecture 11.1 is to attach a long leg to a fixed gadget and to show that the cuts of Remark 6.3 produce all small values. The following observation shows that the attached part can never stay bounded.

Proposition 11.2 (Blocked legs).

Let (K,s)(K,s) be a status-labelled tree in which no vertex has status 𝗂\mathsf{i} or 𝗈\mathsf{o}, and let c∈V⁡(K)c\in V(K) with s⁡(c)=𝗇s(c)=\mathsf{n}. For k≥1k\geq 1, let h⁡(k)h(k) be the Grundy value of KK with a new path c=w0,w1,…,wkc=w_{0},w_{1},\dots,w_{k} attached at cc, where w1,…,wk−1w_{1},\dots,w_{k-1} have status 𝗇\mathsf{n} and wkw_{k} has status 𝗂\mathsf{i}. Then for every k≥2k\geq 2,

h(k)∉{h(k−1)}∪{h(k′),h(k′)⊕1: 1≤k′≤k−2}.h(k)\notin\{h(k-1)\}\cup\{h(k^{\prime}),\,h(k^{\prime})\oplus 1:\ 1\leq k^{\prime}\leq k-2\}.

Consequently each value of ⌊h⁡(k)/2⌋\lfloor h(k)/2\rfloor is taken at most twice, and only at consecutive kk. In particular h⁡(k)→∞h(k)\to\infty.

Proof.

The far end wkw_{k} forces its edge to point towards cc. Let 2≤j≤k2\leq j\leq k and orient wj−1​wjw_{j-1}w_{j} in direction δ\delta, which must point towards cc if j=kj=k. As in Proposition 6.1, the result is the same gadget with a leg of j−1j-1 edges, blocked in direction δ\delta, plus a detached run of k−jk-j edges, which has value Ck−jC_{k-j} or Dk−jD_{k-j} by Theorem 4.3. Reversing all arrows shows that the value of the gadget with a leg of length k′k^{\prime} blocked in either direction is h⁡(k′)h(k^{\prime}), because KK has no vertex of status 𝗂\mathsf{i} or 𝗈\mathsf{o}. For j=kj=k this gives the option h⁡(k−1)⊕C0=h⁡(k−1)h(k-1)\oplus C_{0}=h(k-1). For j≤k−1j\leq k-1, both directions are allowed and {Cm,Dm}={0,1}\{C_{m},D_{m}\}=\{0,1\} for m=k−j≥1m=k-j\geq 1, giving both h⁡(j−1)h(j-1) and h⁡(j−1)⊕1h(j-1)\oplus 1. A Grundy value differs from the values of all options. For the consequence, if ⌊h⁡(k′)/2⌋=⌊h⁡(k)/2⌋\lfloor h(k^{\prime})/2\rfloor=\lfloor h(k)/2\rfloor with k′≤k−2k^{\prime}\leq k-2, then h⁡(k)∈{h⁡(k′),h⁡(k′)⊕1}h(k)\in\{h(k^{\prime}),h(k^{\prime})\oplus 1\}, which is impossible. ∎

So the options t⊕h⁡(z−1−t)t\oplus h(z-1-t) produced by cutting a long leg involve an unbounded function hh. When h⁡(k)=k+ch(k)=k+c for large kk, as in all two-legged gadgets we computed except (1,2​j)(1,2j), these options all have the parity of z−1+cz-1+c; more precisely, they form the set given by the identity {t⊕(n−t):0≤t≤n}={e≤n:e≡n(mod2),e&n−e2=0}\{t\oplus(n-t):0\leq t\leq n\}=\{e\leq n:e\equiv n\pmod{2},\ e\mathbin{\&}\tfrac{n-e}{2}=0\}. This suggests that large Grundy values come from the irregular part of hh at small arguments.

Question 11.3.

Is there a conceptual reason why the two short legs of S⁡(x,y,z)S(x,y,z) become “invisible” when zz is large (Conjecture 7.4)? A natural approach is an analogue of the periodicity theorem for octal games [9, 5]. The difficulty is that some spider states have Grundy values that grow linearly with the length of the long leg, because of the nim heaps Bh=hB_{h}=h; Section 8.4 shows how to deal with this for each fixed pair.

Question 11.4.

Call a thread of a piece internal if both of its ends have degree at least 33, and a leaf thread otherwise. By Corollary 10.4, the parity conjecture holds when all threads have at most two edges. By Theorem 10.11, it can fail when all threads have at most three edges. It can even fail when all internal threads have at most three edges and all leaf threads at most two. To see this, take the piece of T21T_{21}, and at the free end of each of its two legs with three edges attach two new edges to free leaves. The result is a piece with 2020 vertices, 1919 edges and Grundy value 33 (by Theorem 5.6 it is equivalent to the piece of T21T_{21}). Turning it into a tree and attaching a path with two edges at a special vertex (Remark 5.2) gives a counterexample. Does the parity conjecture hold when all internal threads have at most two edges and all leaf threads at most three? A search over the 19,57019{,}570 twin-free pieces of this kind with at most 2222 vertices, other than paths, found no counterexample.

Question 11.5.

The proportion of counterexamples among trees with nn vertices grows from 0.026%0.026\% at n=15n=15 to 0.088%0.088\% at n=20n=20. Does it tend to 1/21/2? Heuristically, by Corollary 3.8, a large random tree is the nim-sum of many small pieces. If pieces with Grundy value at least 22 occur with positive density, the Grundy value of a large random tree should be non-zero with probability tending to 11. Then essentially the trees with m\operatorname{m} even, about half of all trees, would violate the conjecture.

Question 11.6.

Which Grundy values occur for the full Game of Cycles on 22-connected plane graphs? Fokkink and Zandee found the value 33. Are there gadgets analogous to runs (nim heaps) when the cycle rule is present?

Closing remarks

The Game of Cycles was designed to show how much mathematics hides in simple rules, and it keeps that promise. A guess that held on thousands of small trees failed for a reason as old as combinatorial game theory itself: Nim was hiding inside. We hope that the questions above will lead others to play the game and to find more surprises in it.

Data and code availability

The programs (P1)–(P3), the scripts that produce Tables 2, 3, 4 and 5, the certificate and verification programs for Sections 8, 9 and 10, the raw output, and the hand-checkable certificate for S⁡(1,3,7)S(1,3,7) are provided as ancillary files with the arXiv version of this paper (directory anc/); the file anc/README.md explains how to re-run every check.

Use of AI tools

The author used a generative AI system, Claude (Anthropic), for two purposes.

  • •

    Writing. The AI system was used to draft and edit the text of the paper.

  • •

    Computation. The AI system was used to write, run and cross-check the programs behind the computational results, namely the programs (P1)–(P3) of Section 7.1 and the other programs and scripts in the ancillary files. The re-implementations in anc/independent_checks/ were written by separate instances of the AI system from the text of the paper alone, without access to the other programs.

The AI system is not an author of this paper. The author has reviewed the paper and takes full responsibility for its contents.
